stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought in 8 hours after swallowing 30 g of acetaminophen. He has nausea and vomiting, and his aminotransferases are still normal. Two days later they rise steeply as the liver starts to fail.
oneliner: 17M + 30 g acetaminophen 8 h ago + nausea, vomiting + aminotransferases rise at day 2 → which hepatocytes die first?

whyNot.A: Cells beside the portal tract get the **most oxygen** and have little cytochrome P450, so they are **spared** in this overdose
whyNot.B: Intermediate in oxygen and enzyme content; this zone is hit first in **yellow fever**, not here
whyNot.C: Biliary epithelium is injured in **cholestatic disease** with a high alkaline phosphatase, not a steep **aminotransferase rise**
whyNot.E: Macrophages that clear debris; the toxic metabolite is made by **P450 inside hepatocytes**

why: Acetaminophen is converted by **CYP2E1** to the toxic metabolite **NAPQI**, which glutathione normally neutralizes, but a huge dose exhausts glutathione. **Zone 3 hepatocytes** have the most P450 activity and the **lowest oxygen**, so they die first, with aminotransferases peaking at **2-3 days**.

idea.rule: Zone 3 hepatocytes have the most cytochrome P450 and the least oxygen, so toxins and ischemia injure them first.
also: Right heart failure causes centrilobular congestion (nutmeg liver)
Alcoholic hepatitis begins around the central vein
Carbon tetrachloride, activated by P450, also causes centrilobular necrosis
